notes.meaning: Herod the tetrarch heard the news about what Jesus was doing. A tetrarch was a subordinate ruler over a fourth part of a kingdom. Even though Jesus was rejected in his own hometown, his fame reached the royal palace.

Herod told his servants that Jesus must be John the Baptist raised from the dead. Herod's guilty conscience haunted him for killing John, making him terrified of God's power. He believed this resurrection gave Jesus the power to perform great miracles.

Herod had previously arrested John, chained him, and thrown him into prison. He did this because of Herodias, the wife of his half-brother Philip. Herod had taken her away to live with him as his own wife.

John had repeatedly told Herod that taking his brother's wife broke God's law. Even though Herod was a powerful ruler, John refused to soften the truth to stay safe. God's law against adultery and incest applies to kings just as it does to everyone else.

Herod wanted to kill John right away, but he was afraid of the people. The crowds respected John as a true prophet sent by God. Herod was kept from greater violence only because he worried about losing his popularity and facing a revolt.

During a large banquet for Herod's birthday, the daughter of Herodias danced for the guests. Her performance pleased Herod very much. Such a public dance by a royal princess was viewed as shameless and led the king into further temptation.

Herod made a rash promise to the girl and backed it up with a solemn oath. He swore to give her whatever she asked for. Making such a careless vow showed foolish pride and opened the door to great sin.

Coached by her mother, the girl asked for John the Baptist's head on a large platter. Herodias hated John for condemning her unlawful marriage and used her daughter to carry out revenge. The young girl willingly carried out her mother's cruel demand.
Herod felt troubled by the gruesome request, but he ordered it done anyway. He was too proud to break his oath in front of his dinner guests. A sinful promise never justifies committing murder.

Herod sent an officer to the prison, and John was beheaded in secret. The prophet died as a martyr, meaning someone killed for staying faithful to God. Wicked rulers can end an earthly life, but they cannot destroy the eternal reward God gives His servants.

John's head was brought into the feast on a platter and handed to the girl. She carried it straight to her mother, satisfying Herodias's bitter hatred. God permits wicked people a short-lived triumph, but their cruelty brings certain judgment.

John's disciples came to the prison, took his body, and gave it a decent burial. Afterward, they went directly to Jesus to tell Him what had happened. When we face deep sorrow and loss, the best thing to do is carry our grief straight to the Lord.

When Jesus heard about John's death, He got into a boat to find a quiet, lonely place. He wanted to give His disciples rest and avoid unnecessary danger before His proper time had arrived. But the crowds heard where He went and walked around the shore from nearby towns to meet Him.

Stepping ashore, Jesus saw the vast crowd waiting for Him. Instead of feeling frustrated about losing His quiet time, He felt deep compassion for them. Moved by love, He spent the day healing their sick and caring for their needs.

As evening approached, the disciples urged Jesus to send the crowds away to buy food in the villages. They were in a remote place, and the hour was growing late. The disciples saw the huge physical need, but they did not yet expect a miracle.

Jesus told the disciples that the people did not need to leave, and He ordered them to feed the crowd themselves. He gave this command to test their faith and show them their own weakness. When the Lord asks us to do what seems impossible, He intends to provide the answer.

The disciples answered that they only had five loaves of bread and two fish. These were small barley loaves, representing very simple and limited food. They looked at their tiny supply and felt completely unable to help so many people.

Jesus told them to bring whatever they had directly to Him. When we place our small resources in Christ's hands, He can bless them and make them enough. Everything we offer to God becomes fruitful when given in faith.

Jesus told the crowds to recline on the grass like guests at a feast. He took the loaves and fish, looked up toward heaven, and gave thanks to God. Then He broke the loaves and handed them to the disciples, who distributed them to the people.

Everyone in the massive crowd ate until they were completely satisfied. Afterward, the disciples gathered twelve baskets full of leftover broken pieces so nothing would go to waste. This miracle showed that Jesus has the creative power of God and provides abundantly for His people.

About five thousand men were fed, in addition to many women and children. The total size of the gathering was likely much larger. This huge miracle showed the crowds that Jesus had the divine power of the promised Messiah, God's anointed King.

Right after the meal, Jesus made His disciples get into their boat and head across the lake while He dismissed the crowd. The people were eager to make Him an earthly king by force, and He wanted His followers away from that temptation. The disciples obeyed their Master even though they did not want to leave Him behind.

After sending the crowds away, Jesus climbed up the mountain alone to pray. When night fell, He remained there by Himself in quiet conversation with His Father. He set a clear pattern for believers about the importance of getting alone for secret prayer.

Out on the water, the disciples found their boat battered by strong waves in the middle of the lake. A fierce headwind blew against them, making it hard to make progress. Being where Jesus sent them did not keep them from trouble, but He was still watching over them.

Late in the night, between three and six in the morning, Jesus came walking toward them on the water. Walking on the sea proved His divine authority over creation. In Scripture, treading on the waves is a sign of God's almighty power.

When the disciples saw a figure moving across the dark water, they cried out in terror. They assumed they were seeing a ghost or evil spirit. Fear often blinds our eyes so that we fail to recognize Christ when He comes to help us.

Jesus immediately spoke to them, telling them to take courage because it was He, and not to fear. Hearing His voice brought instant relief to their panic. His presence reminded them that God was right beside them in the storm.

Peter spoke up and asked Jesus to command him to walk across the water to meet Him. His request showed deep love and bold faith, mixed with his usual impulsiveness. He wanted to step out on the sea, but he rightly waited for the Lord's command before doing so.

Jesus gave the command to come, and Peter climbed out of the boat and walked on the water toward Him. As long as Peter trusted Christ's word, God's power held him up above the waves. Believers can face trials beyond their natural ability when they walk in obedience to Christ.

When Peter took his eyes off Jesus and looked at the roaring wind and waves, he was gripped with fear and started to sink. In his panic, he cried out a short, desperate prayer: 'Lord, save me!' Looking at our difficulties instead of Christ will quickly sink our courage, but the Lord is always ready to hear our cry.

Jesus instantly stretched out His hand, caught hold of Peter, and gently asked him why he doubted. He showed Peter that his sinking came from weak faith, not from the power of the wind. Jesus does not abandon those whose faith wavers, but He rescues them and teaches them to rely on Him.

As soon as Jesus and Peter climbed up into the boat, the wind suddenly died down. The storm had finished its work of testing the disciples, and Christ's presence brought stillness. When the Lord enters our trials, He commands peace.

Everyone inside the boat fell down and worshiped Jesus, confessing that He truly is the Son of God. Seeing Him master the wind and walk on the sea settled their doubts about His divine nature. Their severe trial ended in heartfelt worship and deeper praise.

After crossing the lake, the boat landed safely at Gennesaret. This was a rich, populated plain on the northwestern shore of the Sea of Galilee. Wherever Jesus traveled, He brought life and help to the people living there.

The local people recognized Jesus at once and quickly sent the news across the entire countryside. Families and neighbors carried all their sick friends directly to Him. Those who know Christ should eagerly tell others so they can find His mercy too.

The people begged Jesus to let the sick merely touch the fringe of His outer garment, and everyone who touched Him was completely cured. The healing power did not come from the cloth itself, but from Christ who rewarded their simple faith. Jesus heals entirely, and He offers that same grace to heal our souls from sin.
